title: Bartik shift-share IV for local employment shock on wages

llm_response.content:
## 1. Identification Strategy
- Method: Two-stage least squares (2SLS) using a Bartik (shift-share) instrument.
- Rationale: Local employment growth (x) is potentially endogenous to local wage changes (y) due to reverse causality and omitted local shocks. The Bartik instrument z combines pre-period local industry shares with national industry growth rates, providing plausibly exogenous variation in local labor demand.
- Key assumptions:
  - Relevance: z is correlated with local employment growth x (national industry growth shifts local employment proportionally to initial industry shares).
  - Exclusion: Conditional on controls (initial wages, population), z affects y only through x (national industry shocks are not driven by local idiosyncratic wage shocks).
  - Predetermined exposure: Initial industry shares are measured prior to the shock period and are not chosen in anticipation of subsequent local wage shocks.
  - Granularity/leave-one-out logic: No single industry dominates the local exposure and local areas do not meaningfully drive national industry growth (so national growth is as-good-as-exogenous to any single local area).
  - SUTVA and correct model specification.

## 2. R Code
```r
# Complete, self-contained R code

# 0) Setup --------------------------------------------------------------------
pkgs <- c("AER", "sandwich", "lmtest")
to_install <- pkgs[!(pkgs %in% installed.packages()[,"Package"])]
if (length(to_install) > 0) install.packages(to_install, repos = "https://cloud.r-project.org")
lapply(pkgs, require, character.only = TRUE)

# 1) Load data ----------------------------------------------------------------
path <- "experiments/exp_b/data/s22_data.csv"
df <- read.csv(path)
df <- na.omit(df)

# Quick check
stopifnot(all(c("y","x","z","controls") %in% names(df)))
N <- nrow(df)

# 2) Core specifications -------------------------------------------------------
# OLS
ols <- lm(y ~ x + controls, data = df)

# First stage: x on z + controls
fs <- lm(x ~ z + controls, data = df)

# Reduced form: y on z + controls
rf <- lm(y ~ z + controls, data = df)

# 2SLS (IV): y on x instrumented by z, with controls included as exogenous
iv <- ivreg(y ~ x + controls | z + controls, data = df)

# Robust (HC1) variance-covariance matrices
vc_ols <- sandwich::vcovHC(ols, type = "HC1")
vc_fs  <- sandwich::vcovHC(fs,  type = "HC1")
vc_rf  <- sandwich::vcovHC(rf,  type = "HC1")
vc_iv  <- sandwich::vcovHC(iv,  type = "HC1")

# Helper to print coefficient results
print_coef <- function(model, vcov_mat, coefname, label) {
  b  <- coef(model)[coefname]
  se <- sqrt(diag(vcov_mat))[coefname]
  t  <- b / se
  p  <- 2 * pnorm(abs(t), lower.tail = FALSE)
  ci <- c(b - 1.96*se, b + 1.96*se)
  cat(sprintf("%s: %s = %.4f (SE=%.4f), 95%% CI [%.4f, %.4f], p=%.4f\n",
              label, coefname, b, se, ci[1], ci[2], p))
}

# First-stage robust F-stat for instrument (single instrument => t^2 on z)
fs_ct <- lmtest::coeftest(fs, vcov. = vc_fs)
t_z   <- as.numeric(fs_ct["z","t value"])
F_fs_robust <- t_z^2

# Also compute the conventional (non-robust) first-stage F using ivreg diagnostics
iv_sum_diag <- summary(iv, diagnostics = TRUE)
weakF_conv <- tryCatch(
  {
    as.numeric(iv_sum_diag$diagnostics["Weak instruments (first-stage F-statistic)", "statistic"])
  },
  error = function(e) NA_real_
)

# 3) Print main results --------------------------------------------------------
cat("Sample size (N):", N, "\n\n")

cat("=== OLS (y ~ x + controls) ===\n")
print_coef(ols, vc_ols, "x", "OLS")

cat("\n=== Reduced Form (y ~ z + controls) ===\n")
print_coef(rf, vc_rf, "z", "Reduced form")

cat("\n=== First Stage (x ~ z + controls) ===\n")
print_coef(fs, vc_fs, "z", "First stage")
cat(sprintf("First-stage robust F (on z): %.2f\n", F_fs_robust))
if (!is.na(weakF_conv)) cat(sprintf("First-stage conventional F (ivreg diagnostics): %.2f\n", weakF_conv))

cat("\n=== 2SLS (IV) (y ~ x + controls | z + controls) ===\n")
print_coef(iv, vc_iv, "x", "2SLS")

# Wu-Hausman endogeneity test (from ivreg diagnostics; note: not robust)
if (!is.null(iv_sum_diag$diagnostics)) {
  # Attempt to extract Wu-Hausman line robustly
  diag_tab <- iv_sum_diag$diagnostics
  wh_row <- grep("Wu-Hausman", rownames(diag_tab))
  if (length(wh_row) == 1) {
    wh_stat <- as.numeric(diag_tab[wh_row, "statistic"])
    wh_p    <- as.numeric(diag_tab[wh_row, "p-value"])
    cat(sprintf("Wu-Hausman endogeneity test: stat=%.3f, p=%.3f (non-robust)\n", wh_stat, wh_p))
  }
}

# 4) Robustness checks ---------------------------------------------------------
cat("\n--- Robustness checks ---\n")

# (a) IV without controls (sensitivity to omitted variables)
iv_noc <- ivreg(y ~ x | z, data = df)
vc_iv_noc <- sandwich::vcovHC(iv_noc, type = "HC1")
print_coef(iv_noc, vc_iv_noc, "x", "2SLS (no controls)")

# (b) Add flexible control (quadratic in controls)
iv_poly <- ivreg(y ~ x + controls + I(controls^2) | z + controls + I(controls^2), data = df)
vc_iv_poly <- sandwich::vcovHC(iv_poly, type = "HC1")
print_coef(iv_poly, vc_iv_poly, "x", "2SLS (controls + controls^2)")

# (c) Trim extreme outliers in x and y (1% tails) and re-estimate IV
qx <- quantile(df$x, c(0.01, 0.99), na.rm = TRUE)
qy <- quantile(df$y, c(0.01, 0.99), na.rm = TRUE)
trim_idx <- with(df, x >= qx[1] & x <= qx[2] & y >= qy[1] & y <= qy[2])
df_trim <- df[trim_idx, ]
iv_trim <- ivreg(y ~ x + controls | z + controls, data = df_trim)
vc_iv_trim <- sandwich::vcovHC(iv_trim, type = "HC1")
cat(sprintf("Trimmed sample size (N): %d\n", nrow(df_trim)))
print_coef(iv_trim, vc_iv_trim, "x", "2SLS (trim 1% tails of x and y)")
```

## 3. Expected Findings
- Sign: Positive. Local labor demand shocks (higher employment growth) should raise wages as firms bid up labor, especially in the short-to-medium run with imperfect labor supply elasticity across local markets.
- Magnitude: An elasticity around 0.1 to 0.3 is typical in the literature; with these data I expect a 2SLS coefficient on x in the neighborhood of 0.2 (i.e., 1% higher employment growth increases wages by about 0.2%). OLS may be biased downward (e.g., if negative supply shocks simultaneously reduce wages and employment) or upward (if positive local productivity shocks raise both), hence the value of the Bartik IV. The first-stage F should be comfortably above 10 if the instrument is strong.

_ground_truth.identification_strategy: IV/2SLS — Bartik shift-share instrument; identification from national (exogenous) shifts
_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: Employment growth driven by national shifts raises local wages
